questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I chose Sorbonne, as it has a reputation for being one of the best french schools for humanities, and as I have a personal relation to Paris, where I've been living before. Besides this I wanted to improve my french, which is perfect at Sorbonne as most of the classes and all communication is conducted in french.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I've loved being abroad, learning about the ways university as an institution works in other countries. Though I've come to realize that the education, and the way our system works in Denmark, is much more suitable for the way I learn.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: This was pretty difficult, as Sorbonne doesn't really inform their exchange students that much. You are very much left to figure out things for yourself. On an additional note, it is therefore crucial to speak and understand french on a somewhat good level !

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had an assembly with all the exchange students enrolled at the humanities departement in the beginning of the autumn semester.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: There weren't really any orientation available besides the assembly, which didn't focus that much on the things you actually need to know as an exchange student. If possible before going to Paris, try to engage yourself with knowledge of how the french educational system works, so you won't be too unprepared.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
It's very difficult in Paris, as it's an expensive city and there are a lot of scammers. I've only found housing as I have a network down here, that helped me, but I've ended up paying 900 euros for a small studio the first couple of months. But check out pages like cartedecolocs and such to find some people to live with. Often they have a hard time living with students though, as they don't expect us to have a steady income. In France it's normal to live with your parents throughout your university time, as they often also begin university right out of high school. 
Try your best to reach out in your network, people often know someone who know someone, even outside of Denmark!

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: The condition of the appartements in France are often much worse than what we're used to in Denmark. Also the public transportation system in Paris closes down (Metro, RER and such) pretty early (the latest at 2am on the weekends), so if you decide to live outside of Paris, you'll either end up spending a lot of time in night buses or a lot of money on Uber or Bolt.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The housing available to students are either the "crous" campuses, which they deal out according to your parent's income, therefore it's often difficult for danish students to be offered these places, as the generel danish income is a lot higher than in the countries you are "competing" with. Otherwise you can always check out "le cité universitaire", where there is a lot of cheap housing. You just need to know that it's situated in a pretty boring neighborhood of Paris and close to the outskirts of the city.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Beforehand I knew that I needed to make my own schedule completely. This means you choose your classes and your hours, which is very different from what one is used to from Copenhagen university. Therefore you need to take some time out to really plan a good schedule for yourself. Also, they don't use "det akademiske kvarter" in France, so if you schedule classes back to back, you will running around campus, which is extremely unpractical those weeks where you have exams in all courses, and you miss out on the beginning of some!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You have to fill out a format with the classes and the hours you want, both for travaux dirigées and cours magistral (seminars and lectures). These you send to the person in charge of handling the registrations. As you're an exchange student, you are not officially in their system, therefore everything is handled in hand.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not that much to be quite honest. I've spoken with other students in order to understand the system, but don't worry, it's not that difficult.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I've got pretty much all the classes I wanted. Though the courses are way less ECTS points in France, so you'll probably end up having more courses that you're used to in Denmark. Therefore some of the classes tend to overlap.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Please take the time out to do your research on which teachers, classes and hours are best suiting for you before you actually have to registrer, as it will make it much easier for you in the end.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There were some courses I enjoyed, but most of them seemed to me a bit outdated and not really that relevant for our generation. Remember that France are big on traditions and kind of still conservative in some ways. This reflected on the courses that were available.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: To me some of the courses seemed to be not to be on an educational level that high, as you are mostly just commanded to remember and repeat, and not expected that much to think for yourself. This depends a lot on the teacher though! I would recommend choosing some of the younger teachers, as they are often more up to the beat on how to teach in a more progressive way.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The way french people learn is emphasized on learning and repeating whatever the teacher says, and not to work in a reflecting way yourself. Therefore the teaching style could seem rather dull most of the time, and you are taught not to think outside of the box, which for me was pretty sad and didn't develop my skills in any way. Besides they are still pretty oldschool, so you'll write exams in hand, you'll have a lot of test and in some classes it's even mandatory to present (in french) in front of 50 people.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 2 semesters

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Littératures européennes (L5LM31FR), Littérature, idées, arts (L5LIZ03A), Littérature et société (L5LIZ05A), Littérature française des XIXe et XXe siècles (L5LM84FR), Anglais : Langue, littérature et culture anglophone (L5LI98AN).

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your second semester. *
questions.answer: Littérature française classique et moderne (L6LM36FR), Études comparatistes (L6LI39FR).

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Each term they offer a comparative literature course, where you have to read (or translate) in an original language (this often being german, english and spanish). These courses are the best I've had each term, as they are not as focused on France and the french cultural heritage. I really loved Études comparatistes (L6LI39FR), which dealt with gender and gender representation in the novel from the 20th century (also one of the only classes, where female writers were on the curriculum..)

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I'm not really sure I've really encountered any. I've experience mould in my previous appartement, where cleaning supplies costed a bit extra.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Paris is a really expensive city, which I knew beforehand, as I've lived here before. But one advice I could give, is to live in some of the less expensive neighbourhoods, as it's not only the rent that's cheaper, but also the super markets, cafes and so on.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't really enroll in anything, so difficult to say. There is not much of a social life on Sorbonne, so don't expect to go to a Friday's bar or even a student cafe. I think it's possible to do some sports through the university, but I didn't do it myself.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: I think they do something called "parismus", which is like a social thing for erasmus students, where they can meet and engage with other fellow exchange students. I never attended, so I can't say that much about it.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I don't have any thing to recommend regarding what the school offers, but it's a good way to engage with the local community to sign up for anything really, yoga, tennis, drawing classes, whatever you like, to actually meet some french people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Paris has so much to offer, that you sometimes forget how central in Europe you are. It's easy to go on day trips in ile-de-france (the region, where Paris is located), go to the beach in normandy, or even take the train to Amsterdam. With the TGV (fast trains) you can move around in France (and Europe) pretty quickly. Personally I would recommend going to Marseille! It's an amazing city only 3,5 hours from Paris with the TGV.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As I study French language and culture and have lived in Paris before, I would say I'm pretty understanding of the french culture, but I could imagine it being quite a culture clash for some. It's very different from Denmark in a lot of ways. Everything from how poverty is much more evident in Paris to how the french people are actually very conservative in some ways, could be a shock for some.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It's difficult, as french people in some ways are as shy to outsiders as danish people are. But I would say you just have to engage, speak with people in classe, try your best to get out there ! And learn french. French people are sometimes very insecure about their english, and on contrary beliefs, they are not arrogant, but really nice and welcoming !

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Mostly their way of doing exactly what the teachers wants them to do and their lack of trying to think for themselves in class. This was difficult in doing presentations with french people.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I love the french "joie de vivre". Paris is an intoxicating city, where you have endless possibilities of culture and living. To grab a glass of wine after classes, going to museums during the day, reading in parks and just enjoying what the city has to offer.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Know and understand french, even though they tell you it's not crucial, it is. 
Don't expect it to be like it is in Denmark, neither your home, classes or even the people you meet. You're are not in Denmark, so of course things are different from what you are used to. 
Don't do too many classes, try to chose the ones with the high score of ECTS. Often a 4 ECTS point course has at least as heavy a workload as a 8 ECTS point course.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you do your classes in the literature department, you often don't have to do the exams, you're only controlled by the "controle continu", which is controls during the term.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living in Paris, all the cultural possibilities (cheap museums, cheap books etc.), meeting so many great people from all over the world, and really emerging in the language and the culture. Being at Sorbonne is really like being at an oldschool, beautiful campus (as long as you chose courses from the 3rd year of the bachelor).

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Understanding their means of teaching and evaluating you. You really have to work in order not to flunk your classes. It's normal in France to flunk people, which we are not used to in the same extent in Denmark.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
